stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When conservators at a regional archive examined a seventeenth-century coastal chart under ultraviolet light, they found that its coastline had been redrawn at least twice. The revisions, which earlier catalogers had mistaken for water damage, shared one telling feature ______ a faint iron-based ink that the original engraver, working decades earlier, had never used.
explanation: Cross out the interrupter 'which earlier catalogers had mistaken for water damage' and you are left with 'The revisions shared one telling feature.' That is a complete sentence, and it points ahead to a feature it hasn't named yet. What follows is a noun phrase that names it: 'a faint iron-based ink...' The clause 'that the original engraver... had never used' only describes the ink. It doesn't give the phrase its own main verb. A colon is the mark that goes between a complete sentence and the thing it introduces.

A.why: You chose the semicolon because it looks formal. A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides. 'A faint iron-based ink that the original engraver had never used' has no main verb of its own. 'Had never used' belongs to the 'that' clause, so it doesn't count.

C.why: Adding 'it was' turns the second part into a complete sentence, and then a bare comma joins two complete sentences. That's a comma splice.

D.why: A period leaves 'A faint iron-based ink that the original engraver... had never used' standing alone as a sentence. It's a noun phrase with no main verb, so you've made a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Excavators at a Bronze Age settlement in the hills of central Anatolia had long assumed that its residents abandoned the site after a single catastrophic fire. Soil cores taken from beneath the collapsed granaries, however, pointed to something far more gradual ______ a decades-long drop in rainfall that left the surrounding fields, once planted with barley, too dry to farm.
explanation: 'Soil cores... pointed to something far more gradual' is a complete sentence. 'However' sits safely inside it, set off by commas. The sentence ends on 'something far more gradual,' which promises a specific answer. The part after the blank delivers that answer as a noun phrase: 'a decades-long drop in rainfall...' The verb 'left' belongs to the 'that' clause, not to a main clause. A colon is correct because a complete sentence comes before it and a phrase explaining 'something' comes after it.

A.why: You were caught by the semicolon trap. 'A decades-long drop in rainfall that left the fields too dry' looks long enough to be a sentence. But 'left' is inside a 'that' clause, so the phrase has no main verb and can't stand after a semicolon.

B.why: A period makes 'A decades-long drop in rainfall that left...' its own sentence. Without a main verb, it's a fragment.

C.why: 'It was a decades-long drop...' is a complete sentence. Joining it to the complete sentence before it with only a comma creates a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In the 1970s, planners in several Dutch cities began experimenting with the woonerf, or 'living street.' The design, which removed curbs and allowed children, cyclists, and cars to share a single paved surface, rested on one counterintuitive premise ______ the idea that drivers who feel uncertain about where they may go will slow down on their own.
explanation: Cross out the long 'which' interrupter, which is closed by its second comma, and you have 'The design rested on one counterintuitive premise.' That is a complete sentence that sets up an unnamed premise. What follows, 'the idea that drivers... will slow down,' is a noun phrase that states the premise. The verbs 'feel' and 'will slow' sit inside the 'that' and 'who' clauses. A single dash works like a colon here: it introduces the explanation.

B.why: You picked the semicolon because it seemed to fit a formal sentence. The text after the blank begins with 'the idea that...', which is a noun phrase, not an independent clause. A semicolon can't introduce it.

C.why: 'This was the idea that drivers... will slow down' is a full sentence. Putting it after a complete sentence with only a comma creates a comma splice.

D.why: A period cuts off 'The idea that drivers who feel uncertain... will slow down on their own' as its own sentence. It's a noun plus a 'that' clause with no main verb, so it's a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Marine biologists tracking cleaner wrasse on a reef off the coast of East Africa noticed that the fish, which normally groom any visitor that arrives at their stations, did not treat every client the same way. The wrasse reserved their most careful work for a single group ______ the large, wide-ranging predators that could easily swim off to a rival station if the service displeased them.
explanation: 'The wrasse reserved their most careful work for a single group' is a complete sentence, and 'a single group' needs to be identified. 'The large, wide-ranging predators that could easily swim off...' identifies it. It's a noun phrase, and its verb 'could swim' belongs to the 'that' clause. A colon correctly joins a complete sentence to the phrase that specifies what it set up.

A.why: This is the semicolon trap. The words after the blank are a noun phrase with a 'that' clause attached, not an independent clause. A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides.

B.why: 'They were the large, wide-ranging predators...' is a complete sentence. A bare comma can't join it to the complete sentence before it, so this is a comma splice.

D.why: A period leaves 'The large, wide-ranging predators that could easily swim off...' as a sentence with no main verb. That's a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Agronomists comparing two plots of sorghum in a semiarid field trial found that the plot yielding more grain had received no additional fertilizer and no extra irrigation. The difference, the researchers concluded after three growing seasons, came down to one inexpensive practice ______ a layer of crop residue that farmers had left on the soil surface after harvest instead of burning it.
explanation: Remove the interrupter 'the researchers concluded after three growing seasons' and you have 'The difference came down to one inexpensive practice.' That is a complete sentence that points ahead to a practice it hasn't named. 'A layer of crop residue that farmers had left...' names the practice. 'Farmers had left' is a subject and verb, but they sit inside a 'that' clause modifying 'layer,' so the whole thing is still a noun phrase. A colon introduces it correctly.

A.why: A period makes 'A layer of crop residue that farmers had left...' a separate sentence. The noun 'layer' never gets a main verb, so you've created a fragment.

C.why: You saw 'farmers had left' and took the second part for a full clause, so you reached for a semicolon. That subject and verb belong to a 'that' clause describing 'layer,' and a semicolon can't introduce a noun phrase.

D.why: 'It was a layer of crop residue...' is an independent clause. Joining it to another independent clause with only a comma is a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Engineers reinforcing a nineteenth-century masonry viaduct in northern England faced a problem that modern steel bridges rarely present. Any repair, as their report to the regional rail authority explained in some detail, had to satisfy two competing demands ______ enough added strength to carry today's heavier freight trains and enough flexibility to let the old stone arches keep shifting with the seasons.
explanation: Cross out the interrupter 'as their report... explained in some detail' and you have 'Any repair had to satisfy two competing demands.' That is a complete sentence that promises to name two things. What follows names them as two noun phrases joined by 'and': 'enough added strength...' and 'enough flexibility...' Neither has a main verb, since 'to carry' and 'to let' are infinitives. A colon is the correct way to introduce them.

B.why: You chose the semicolon because the sentence is long and formal. The second part is a pair of noun phrases with infinitives, not an independent clause, so a semicolon isn't allowed here.

C.why: 'These were enough added strength... and enough flexibility...' is a complete sentence. Attaching it to the first complete sentence with only a comma creates a comma splice.

D.why: A period leaves 'Enough added strength to carry... and enough flexibility to let...' standing alone. It has no main verb, so it's a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Forecasters had predicted only light flurries for the lakeshore town that January evening, yet by midnight nearly forty centimeters of snow had fallen. A review by the regional weather office, published the following spring, traced the error to a factor its computer models had underweighted ______ the unusually warm surface of the lake, which was still several degrees above its seasonal average.
explanation: Skip the interrupter 'published the following spring' and you have 'A review traced the error to a factor its computer models had underweighted.' That is a complete sentence that ends by pointing to an unnamed factor. 'The unusually warm surface of the lake, which was still several degrees above...' names the factor. It's a noun phrase, and the verb 'was' belongs to the 'which' clause. A colon connects the complete sentence to the phrase that explains it.

A.why: This is the semicolon trap. The 'which was still...' clause makes the second part look like a sentence, but its only verb is inside that relative clause. 'The unusually warm surface' itself has no main verb, so a semicolon can't come before it.

B.why: 'It was the unusually warm surface of the lake' is a complete sentence. A comma alone can't join it to the complete sentence before the blank, so this is a comma splice.

C.why: A period turns 'The unusually warm surface of the lake, which was still...' into a sentence of its own. The main noun never gets a verb, so you've written a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Field linguists documenting a small language of the Amazon basin were initially puzzled that its speakers almost never used words for left and right. Recordings of everyday conversation, collected over two years in three neighboring villages, eventually revealed what speakers relied on instead ______ a system of directions anchored to the flow of the nearest river.
explanation: Without the interrupter 'collected over two years in three neighboring villages,' the core is 'Recordings eventually revealed what speakers relied on instead.' That is a complete sentence that names a mystery without answering it. The answer comes after the blank as a noun phrase: 'a system of directions anchored to the flow of the nearest river.' 'Anchored' is a participle, not a main verb. A colon is the mark that says 'here it is.'

A.why: Adding 'it was' makes the second part an independent clause. A bare comma between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

B.why: You chose the semicolon because it looks like the formal choice. 'A system of directions anchored to the flow of the nearest river' has no main verb ('anchored' only modifies 'directions'), and a semicolon needs a full clause on both sides.

D.why: A period makes 'A system of directions anchored to the flow of the nearest river' its own sentence. It has no main verb, so it's a fragment.
